newsitem.title: USA: Hotel vacancies drop, and stocks rise - Barron's.
newsitem.headline: Hotel vacancies drop, and stocks rise - Barron's.

text.p: As go occupancy rates, so go stock prices. And right now, hotel companies are seeing business surging and their investors are seeing stock prices rising, according to a report in Barron's.

In Sunday's edition of the financial news tabloid, the increase in business began in 1993 as the industry recovered from a slump that was caused partly by overbuilding and loose financing in the 1980s, and a recession from the early 1990s.
Occupancy rates are now at 65 percent nationally and rising room rates have increased revenues per room.

Since January, Marriott International Inc's stock has risen 22 percent; Promus Hotel Corp's is up 36 percent; CapStar Hotel Co's has increased 64 percent; Hilton's is up 16 percent; ITT Corp's has risen 48 percent; Prime Hospitality Corp shares are up 18 percent; and Four Seasons Hotels Inc has increased 70 percent based on U.S. dollars, Barron's said.
While the hotel boom is good for investors, it's not necessarily welcome news for guests.
The lower vacancy rates, particularly in larger U.S. cities such as New York and Chicago, are prompting some hotel companies to reconsider their strategies, Barron's said.
For example, Hilton Hotels Corp's Waldorf-Astoria is considering requiring a three-day minimum stay for guests who do not reserve a room well in advance, Barron's said.
